Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A striped hot air balloon floating over a lavender field at sunset, with purple hills, a golden hill, and a lone tree on the right.

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

12 stepsFocal point: The striped balloon in the upper left, with the setting sun just below the middle as a second bright spot. Light: The sun sets low in the center (43% across, 41% down), lighting the clouds pink and orange from below, the golden hill warm gold, and the left side of the tree's crown.How this lesson was made

What you need

Tubes

  • Titanium white
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)
  • Ultramarine blue
  • Burnt sienna

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: the whole sky gradientFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #10 filbert: scrubbing in the cloud masses and streaksFilbert: flat with a rounded end, for soft-edged shapes
  • #6 round: filling the sun diskRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 3/4 inch flat: the mountain shapesFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • old stiff flat: dabbing the bumpy tree rowsOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • #6 filbert: small dabs in the far rowsFilbert: flat with a rounded end, for soft-edged shapes
  • #4 round: the narrow edge stripes, basket, and ropesRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press

Also

  • White canvas or canvas board
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

The steps

Step 1Step 2Step 3Step 4Step 5Step 6Step 7Step 8Step 9Step 10Step 11Step 12

STEP 1 OF 12

Paint the sunset sky

  1. Load the 1 inch flat with Sky blue and paint long side-to-side strokes across the top tenth of the canvas.
  2. Below the blue, paint Sunset orange in long strokes, blending up into the blue while both are wet so it turns a soft violet where they meet.
  3. Brush Sunset gold in a wide oval glow a little left of center, a bit below the middle of the sky, and blend its edges into the orange.
  4. Keep the orange going down to about 6/10 of the way down the canvas, with a straight bottom edge. Leave the bottom 4/10 white.
Paints for this step3 paints, 3 new
  • Sky blue new3 parts white, 2 parts ultramarine, a touch of burnt sienna
  • Sunset orange new2 parts red, 1 part yellow, 1 part white
  • Sunset gold new3 parts yellow, 2 parts red, 2 parts white

Brushes

1 inch flat

Strokes

Long side-to-side strokes. Pull the flat across the full width in one go, then go back over the line where two colors meet with a lightly loaded brush until it's soft.

X stroke. Around the gold glow, criss-cross small X shapes so the gold melts into the orange with no hard edge.

Watch out: Stopping the sky at the hill line. Run it lower; the mountains and fields cover it later.

Watch out: Overworking the blend until it's muddy. A few passes are enough.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 12

Dab in the big clouds

  1. With the filbert and Coral pink, scrub in a big cloud mass over the upper right, from the middle of the canvas to the right edge and from the top down to about a third.
  2. Scrub a smaller pink cloud group on the upper left, from the left edge to about a fifth across, and leave the blue showing in the top middle.
  3. Drag a few long, thin pink-orange streaks across the sky below the clouds, down to just above the glow.
  4. Dab Peach light on the tops of the cloud masses, where the sun lights them.
Paints for this step3 paints, 2 new
  • Coral pink new3 parts red, 2 parts white, 1 part ultramarine
  • Sunset orange from step 1, mix more if it has dried2 parts red, 1 part yellow, 1 part white
  • Peach light new6 parts white, 3 parts yellow, 2 parts red, 1 part burnt sienna

Brushes

#10 filbert

Strokes

Dabbing. Push the filbert's rounded tip into the canvas in short scrubby strokes, overlapping them so the cloud builds into one soft lumpy mass.

Long side-to-side strokes. For the streaks, lay the filbert flat and pull it sideways with light pressure so the stroke thins out at each end.

Watch out: Making lots of small separate puffs. Keep the clouds as two big masses and a few streaks.

Watch out: Covering the gold glow. Keep the streaks thin near the middle so the glow stays bright.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 3 OF 12

Paint the sun

  1. Load the #6 round with Sun cream and paint a small solid circle in the brightest part of the glow, a little left of center and about 4/10 of the way down.
  2. Make it about one-twenty-fifth of the canvas width across.
  3. With a dry, clean brush, lightly soften the edge so it glows into the gold.
Paints for this step1 paint, 1 new
  • Sun cream new6 parts white, 3 parts yellow, 1 part red

Brushes

#6 round

Strokes

Press and lift. Press the round down in the middle of the circle and work outward in small curved strokes, lifting at the edge to keep it round.

Dry brushing. Wipe the brush almost dry and lightly brush around the rim so the cream feathers into the gold.

Watch out: Making the sun too big. It's only about the width of a fingertip on a 16 x 24 inch canvas.

Watch out: Thin paint. Use it thick so the orange doesn't show through.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 4 OF 12

Paint the far mountains

  1. Paint the far mountains in Mountain purple across the whole width: a rounded peak on the left about 4/10 down, dipping down right over the bottom half of the sun.
  2. Rise again to a second ridge right of center, and keep the ridge going at about the same height to the right edge.
  3. Fill the mountains down to about half way down the canvas.
  4. Blend a little Sunset orange into the purple near the sun, where the glow lights the slopes. The orange sky still shows below the mountains.
Paints for this step2 paints, 1 new
  • Mountain purple new1 part ultramarine, 1 part white, a touch of red
  • Sunset orange from step 1, mix more if it has dried2 parts red, 1 part yellow, 1 part white

Brushes

3/4 inch flat

Strokes

Horizontal strokes. Cut the ridge line with the flat's edge, then fill below it with short sideways strokes that follow the slope.

Wet blending. While the purple is wet, touch a little Sunset orange in near the sun and stroke it in sideways until it fades into the purple.

Watch out: Hard, sharp ridge lines. Far mountains look softer and lighter than near ones.

Watch out: Leaving the whole sun showing. The ridge dips over its lower half, so it looks like it's setting.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 5 OF 12

Paint the golden fields and hill

  1. Paint a band of Field gold across the left half, just under the mountains, about half way down the canvas.
  2. Paint the big golden hill on the right: start low near the left third and sweep it up to the right edge, where its top is just below the mountains.
  3. Run the gold down to a straight edge a little more than 6/10 of the way down everywhere, past where the lavender will start.
  4. Drag a little Sunset orange along the lower slope of the hill for a warm shadow.
Paints for this step2 paints, 1 new
  • Field gold new3 parts yellow, 1 part red, a touch of ultramarine
  • Sunset orange from step 1, mix more if it has dried2 parts red, 1 part yellow, 1 part white

Brushes

1 inch flat

Strokes

Horizontal strokes. Lay the left field in with sideways strokes across the canvas.

Strokes that follow the hill. On the hill, pull the flat diagonally up and to the right along the slope so the strokes show the hill rising.

Dry brushing. With very little Sunset orange on the brush, skim over the lower slope so it catches on the canvas texture.

Watch out: Stopping right at the lavender line. Run the gold a little lower; the lavender covers it.

Watch out: Flat, even gold. Let some orange and lighter gold strokes show so the hill looks like grass.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 6 OF 12

Dab the tree lines

  1. Dab a thin row of small Tree green bumps along the bottom of the mountains, from the left edge to past the middle, so it ends against the golden hill.
  2. Dab a nearer, taller row of rounded bushy bumps across the left half, along the bottom of the left field.
  3. Touch a little Sunlit green on a few of the tops. Leave the golden hill on the right bare.

  • Tree green new3 parts ultramarine, 1 part yellow, a touch of red, a touch of white
  • Sunlit green new1 part yellow, 1 part burnt sienna, a touch of ultramarine

Brushes

old stiff flat#6 round

Strokes

Dabbing. Load the corner of the stiff brush and tap it straight down, moving along the row, so each tap leaves a little rounded bump.

Watch out: Painting single trees. Keep it a bumpy row, not separate trees.

Watch out: Making the far row as big as the near one. Farther away means smaller.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 7 OF 12

Paint the lone tree

  1. Pull the trunk up from the top of the golden hill, near the right edge (about 85% across), in Trunk brown: wide at the base, then splitting into two or three branches.
  2. Build the crown in Tree green as three or four overlapping round clusters of dabs: one on the left, a higher one in the middle, one on the right, and one along the bottom.
  3. Make the crown about half again as wide as it is tall, reaching up to about a fifth of the way down the canvas.
  4. Leave a gap or two at the bottom of the crown where the branches show.
Paints for this step2 paints, 1 new
  • Trunk brown new2 parts ultramarine, 2 parts burnt sienna, 1 part red, a touch of white
  • Tree green from step 6, mix more if it has dried3 parts ultramarine, 1 part yellow, a touch of red, a touch of white

Brushes

#6 roundold stiff flat

Strokes

Pulling and tapering. Press the round down at the base of the trunk and pull upward, lifting as you go so each branch ends thin.

Dabbing. Tap the stiff brush around each cluster, working from the middle out, so the edges look leafy and lumpy.

Watch out: A lollipop tree (a ball on a stick). Make the crown out of lumpy clusters, wider than tall.

Watch out: A trunk as thick at the top as the bottom. Taper it as it rises.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 8 OF 12

Block in the lavender rows and paths

  1. Find the spot where the two paths meet: at the top of the field, a little right of center (about 6/10 across).
  2. From that spot, paint two Path brown paths down to the bottom edge: the left one landing a little left of center (about a third across), the right one landing near the right side (about 8/10 across). Each is a thin point at the top and a wide strip at the bottom.
  3. Fill the row between the paths with Lavender dark, then the rows beside them: long dark bands that slant toward the meeting spot.
  4. Make the rows thinner and closer together near the top of the field, and wide at the bottom. Cover all the white.
Paints for this step2 paints, 2 new
  • Path brown new2 parts burnt sienna, 1 part red, 1 part white
  • Lavender dark new3 parts ultramarine, 1 part white, a touch of red, a touch of burnt sienna

Brushes

1 inch flat#10 filbert

Strokes

Strokes that follow the paths. Start each path stroke at the bottom edge with the flat pressed wide and pull up toward the meeting spot, lifting so it narrows.

Horizontal strokes. Fill each row with strokes that run along it, slanting toward the meeting spot, so the rows look like they go back into the distance.

Watch out: Paths that stay the same width. They must narrow to a point near the top of the field.

Watch out: Adding texture now. This step is flat dark purple; the dabs come next.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

Why this step, now: The lavender is the nearest part of the scene. The flat dark base and the path layout come first, so the dabs have something to sit on and the perspective is set before any texture.

STEP 9 OF 12

Dab the lavender

  1. Load the filbert with Lavender mid and press short dabs along each row, pointing slightly upward, following the row's slant toward the meeting point.
  2. In the front rows at the bottom of the canvas, make big dabs; in the far rows near the top of the field, make small ones.
  3. Leave the bottom edge of each row dark so the rows look rounded.
  4. Keep the paths brown; don't dab into them.
Paints for this step1 paint, 1 new
  • Lavender mid new3 parts ultramarine, 2 parts white, 1 part red

Brushes

#10 filbert#6 filbert

Strokes

Dabbing. Press the filbert flat onto the row and flick it up a little as you lift, so each dab looks like a tuft of lavender. Work along the row in clusters.

Watch out: Covering the dark base. The dark shows between the dabs and makes the rows look round.

Watch out: Same-size dabs everywhere. Big in front, small at the back.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 11 OF 12

Paint the striped balloon

  1. In the upper left (its middle about 28% across), sketch the balloon lightly: a big circle for the top, tapering down to a short neck about a quarter of the way down the canvas. It's about as wide as it is tall.
  2. Paint a teal stripe straight down the middle, from the top to the neck.
  3. Paint the stripes on each side as curved bands, like ( ) around the middle one: yellow, then red at the edges. They get thinner as they curve around the sides.
  4. Paint a small square basket in Trunk brown just below the neck, with a few thin lines up to the neck for ropes.

Brushes

#6 round#4 round

Strokes

Building a shape from simple pieces. Draw the circle first, then the two curves down to the neck; the stripes then hug the middle stripe like parentheses.

Pulling and tapering. Pull each stripe from the top down to the neck in one curved stroke, pressing harder in the middle where it's widest and lifting at the neck.

Watch out: Straight, parallel stripes. The stripes bend around the balloon, so the outer ones curve the most and get thin.

Watch out: A round ball. The bottom narrows to a neck, like an upside-down teardrop.

Heads up, this picture is a little off: Found in the beginner check, not by a review: the balloon step has six wide stripes (red, yellow, teal, red, yellow, red), while the finish has narrower stripes with teal along both outer edges. The final step's words tell the painter to add the edge stripes, so the pictures and words agree, but the stripe pattern does change between the two images. Paint what the steps say.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 12 OF 12

Final details and highlights

  1. Add a teal stripe down each outer edge of the balloon and a thin orange-red stripe beside the right-hand yellow, so the stripes get narrower toward the sides.
  2. Darken the balloon's left and right edges a little with Balloon teal and Lavender dark, and add a few lighter streaks down the middle of the stripes.
  3. Tap Sunlit green on the left side and top of the tree's crown, where the sun hits it.
  4. Step back and stop. Don't add light everywhere.

Sunset orange plus a little Balloon red for the thin balloon stripe

Brushes

#4 roundold stiff flat

Strokes

Pulling and tapering. Pull the new edge stripes from the top of the balloon down to the neck, following its curve.

Dry brushing. With very little paint, skim darker color along the balloon's edges so it looks round.

Dabbing. Tap the stiff brush lightly on the crown's left side so yellow-green clusters sit on top of the dark green.

Watch out: Adding highlights everywhere. Keep them to the sunlit sides.

Watch out: Fussing with the lavender. It's done; the last touches go on the balloon and tree.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A striped hot air balloon over a lavender field at sunset, with hills, a golden hill, and a lone tree.

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: No bars, borders, captions, or page around it; the whole image is the painting.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: Tiny separate things: yes, a village of houses with cypress trees, scattered bushes on the golden hill, and the balloon's ropes. Textures of hundreds of items: yes, thousands of lavender stalks. Detail inside big shapes: yes, veined, many-puffed clouds and a lake glint. Parts: about 12 at different distances (sky, clouds, sun, mountains, lake, village, middle fields, tree lines, golden hill, tree, lavender, balloon), more than the budget of 8.

Changed: Dropped: the village and its cypresses, the lake glint, the bushes on the golden hill, the ropes. Merged: the clouds into one big upper-right mass, one upper-left group, and a few streaks; the far mountains into one smooth band; the middle distance into one gold field with a dabbed tree line. Turned into marks: the lavender into rows of loose purple dabs, darker at the base, no stalks; the tree's crown into clustered dabs; the golden hill into loose strokes.

Why: With the village gone and the lavender as dabs, every part is either a big shape or one repeated mark, and the lavender can be split into three passes.

A painter's read: a classic sunset paint-along. The sky is the biggest area and sets the mood, a striped balloon is the focal point, and a lavender field with converging paths fills the bottom 4/10. What's hard for a beginner is the lavender (the original has thousands of stalks), the village and scattered bushes in the middle distance, and keeping the balloon's stripes curved. The lesson should be about blending a sunset, then building the lavender in three passes of dabs.

Subject: A striped hot air balloon floating over a lavender field at sunset, with purple hills, a golden hill, and a lone tree on the right.
Focal point: The striped balloon in the upper left, with the setting sun just below the middle as a second bright spot.
Light: The sun sets low in the center (43% across, 41% down), lighting the clouds pink and orange from below, the golden hill warm gold, and the left side of the tree's crown.

What it saw, back to front

  1. sunset sky gradient (blue top, orange and gold glow near the sun)
  2. big pink and orange clouds
  3. the sun
  4. far purple mountains
  5. golden fields and the golden hill
  6. dark green tree lines
  7. the lone tree on the hill
  8. lavender rows and the two paths
  9. the striped balloon and basket
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front

Claude chose it; no technique was named.

ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

Paint-along fits: a sunset sky, far mountains, fields, a tree, and a dabbed lavender field are exactly what YouTube-style back-to-front tutorials teach, each part goes straight over the one behind it, and the white ground is covered by the sky and lavender. Each step is one brush move a beginner can copy.

Passed onBlock in, then build up

It starts with a toned canvas and a sketch, then blocks in flat shapes and builds them up in layers. This picture's look comes from a blended sky and repeated dabs painted straight on, which paint-along teaches directly; the extra tone, sketch, and build-up stages add steps a beginner doesn't need here, and the owner follows paint-along tutorials (decisions, 2026-10-19).

How the paint recipes were worked out18 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Why the steps go in this order12 steps

Back to front: the sky first, run down past the hills to where the lavender starts so its strokes stay long; then the clouds and sun on the sky, the far mountains over the sun's lower half, the golden fields, the tree lines and the tree on the hill. The lavender goes on in three passes (flat dark rows and paths, mid purple dabs, light dabs) so no step jumps from flat to dense texture. The balloon is the subject, so it goes on after the scene with its shading and the tree's sunlit side as the last touches.

  1. 1. Paint the sunset sky

    Everything else sits on the sky, so it goes first and runs down to where the lavender starts.

  2. 2. Dab in the big clouds

    The clouds sit on the sky and behind the balloon and tree, so they go on while the sky is the only layer.

  3. 3. Paint the sun

    The sun is behind the mountains, so it has to be on the canvas before the ridge covers its lower half.

  4. 4. Paint the far mountains

    The farthest land, behind the fields and tree lines.

  5. 5. Paint the golden fields and hill

    The golden fields and hill are the ground the tree lines and tree stand on.

  6. 6. Dab the tree lines

    The tree rows sit on the fields in the middle distance, in front of the mountains.

  7. 7. Paint the lone tree

    The lone tree stands on the golden hill, so the hill has to be there first. Its sunlit side is saved for the last step.

  8. 8. Block in the lavender rows and paths

    The lavender is the nearest part of the scene. The flat dark base and the path layout come first, so the dabs have something to sit on and the perspective is set before any texture.

  9. 9. Dab the lavender

    The first texture pass: one kind of mark, mid purple dabs, so the step isn't a jump from flat rows to dense lavender.

  10. 10. Add light to the lavender

    The second texture pass: light dabs on the row tops, kept separate so each row reads dark, mid, light.

  11. 11. Paint the striped balloon

    The focal point, painted as a flat striped shape over the finished sky, as a teacher would block in the subject.

  12. 12. Final details and highlights

    The balloon's edge stripes and shading and the tree's sunlit side are the last touches, and they end in the finished painting.

Where Claude drew diagrams3 steps, free

Three steps build a shape a beginner would have to work out: the tree's forking trunk and clustered crown, the lavender field's paths meeting at one point, and the balloon's curved stripes. The rest are fills, gradients, or one repeated mark that the words cover. While checking, the balloon step showed fewer, wider stripes than the finish, so the last step's words now say to add the edge stripes.

  • Step 7: Paint the lone tree beginner check

    Noticed: The tree appears whole in one step, and where the trunk forks and how the crown is built isn't clear from the picture; beginners paint a ball on a stick.

    Pieces: A short tapering trunk on the hill, then two or three Y branches, then three round clusters on top and one along the bottom, so the crown comes out lumpy and about one and a half times as wide as tall, as in the step image.

  • Step 8: Block in the lavender rows and paths beginner check

    Noticed: The rows and paths only look right if they all head to one point; placement depends on the perspective, and a beginner would paint parallel stripes.

    Pieces: One meeting point at the top of the field about 60% across, then two wedge-shaped paths opening to the bottom edge, then the rest filled dark with the row edges aimed at the same point (a first try drew the rows as separate bands with white between them, which the step image doesn't have, so the last panel fills everything). The diagram's box is the lavender field only (the bottom 4/10 of the canvas), stretched taller so the rows are readable.

  • Step 11: Paint the striped balloon beginner check

    Noticed: The balloon is a shaped object that appears whole in one step, and its stripes have to curve around it; straight stripes make it look flat.

    Pieces: A circle for the top tapering to a neck (an upside-down teardrop), a straight middle stripe, curved stripes hugging it like ( ), then the basket and ropes. Built the way a teacher draws a balloon, so the stripes follow the round form.

Looked at and left without one

  • Step 1: A gradient from blue to orange to gold; the words give where each color goes.
  • Step 2: Two big masses and a few streaks made by one scrubbing mark; the words give where.
  • Step 3: A small circle; the words give where and how big.
  • Step 4: A soft band with two rounded ridges; the words give the ridge heights.
  • Step 5: Two flat gold areas, the hill described by where it starts and ends.
  • Step 6: A row of repeated dabs, one mark.
  • Step 9: One repeated dab along rows already laid out.
  • Step 10: One repeated light dab on the row tops.
  • Step 12: Small touches on the balloon edges and the crown's sunlit side; the words say where.

A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

  • Round 2 Step 3: After the first redo the sky still stopped at about 55% down, leaving a wider white band than the steps around it. (redone)
  • Round 2 Step 11: Found in the beginner check, not by a review: the balloon step has six wide stripes (red, yellow, teal, red, yellow, red), while the finish has narrower stripes with teal along both outer edges. What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • Steps that keep white canvas below the sky (the sky runs to 62% here) tend to have the render cut the sky short; saying 'a straight lower edge at 62% down' in looks_like from the start might save the redos.
  • A subject added late (the balloon) can come out with a different stripe pattern than the finish; spelling out the finish's stripe order in looks_like would keep them matched.
